title: AI Mortality Models Collapse When Moved Between Hospitals, Study Warns
source_used: Bioengineer.org (carrying Scienmag's report of the Frontiers in Digital Health study)
key_facts: Study in Frontiers in Digital Health by Jorge Robalino-Díaz, William Villegas-Ch and colleagues, Universidad de Las Américas, Quito
Three ICU mortality models (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting) were trained on one database and tested on the other (MIMIC-III and eICU)
Transfer eICU to MIMIC: AUC only 0.598 to 0.642, near coin-flip 0.5
Random forest predicted no deaths at all after transfer, missing all 33 deaths
Gradient boosting caught 2 of 33 deaths; logistic regression caught 18 but wrongly flagged 33 of 77 survivors
MIMIC to eICU: logistic regression caught 44 of 117 deaths with 422 false alarms
Small, retrospective sample (110 MIMIC episodes, 1,324 eICU); authors call results exploratory
quote_evidence: Machine-learning models that promise to forecast which intensive-care patients will die may look impressive on paper and fail completely the moment they are moved to a different hospital.
Random Forest, despite its respectable AUC, produced no positive predictions at all after transfer: every single MIMIC patient was classified as a survivor, including all 33 who died.

the analysis is retrospective, so the authors frame their results as exploratory evidence of threshold-specific instability under dataset shift rather than a definitive estimate of deployment performance.
why_it_matters_hint: Scores that look good in the developer's own data can hide models that miss deaths at another hospital.
notes: Bioengineer.org republishes Scienmag (Ophelia Keating, 15 Oct 2026). Publication date of the study itself not stated.
